question: Should Arjuna fight the battle in which his elders, teachers and kinsmen stand on the other side?

sides.position: He should not fight: killing his own people brings no good and only sin; he would rather live on alms, or be killed unresisting.
arguments: No good is seen in killing one's own people; he wants neither victory, kingship nor pleasures (1.31–35).
Sin would come upon them even for killing aggressors; they should see the fault and turn back (1.36–39, 1.45).
Destroying a family destroys its eternal dharmas, lets adharma prevail, corrupts the women, mixes the classes, deprives the ancestors of their offerings and leads to hell (1.40–44).
It would be better to be killed unarmed and unresisting (1.46), or to live on alms than to kill venerable elders and enjoy blood-smeared pleasures (2.5).
It is not known which outcome is better; they would not wish to live after killing them (2.6); no kingdom would dispel his grief (2.8).

sides.position: He should fight, as his own dharma, without grief and without attachment.
arguments: His faintness is unworthy of the noble, does not lead to heaven and brings disgrace (2.2–3).
The wise do not grieve: the embodied one is eternal and neither slays nor is slain; only bodies perish (2.11–25, 2.30).
Even if the self were born and died again and again, death is certain for the born, so grief is unfit (2.26–28).
For a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma; refusing brings sin and disgrace worse than death (2.31–37).
Fighting with pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat made the same incurs no sin (2.38).
Renouncing all actions in Kṛṣṇa, free of expectation and 'mine', fight (3.30).

notes: A text-internal debate, recorded as the Gītā presents it. Arjuna's acceptance comes only at the end of the Gītā (18.73, outside this chunk). In ch. 1–3 Kṛṣṇa does not answer the family-dharma argument point by point; at 3.24 he says that if he did not act he would be the maker of saṅkara.

question: Are the Vedic rites that hold out heaven, enjoyment and power all there is to seek ('there is nothing else')?

sides.party: Those who delight in the words of the Veda (vedavādaratāḥ), as the Gītā reports them (BhG 2.42–43)
sides.position: There is nothing else: the Veda's speech, abounding in specific rites, is directed to heaven, enjoyment and power, with rebirth as the fruit of action.
arguments: Stated only through the Gītā's description of them: they are intent on heaven, full of desire, and hold that there is nothing beyond (2.42–43).
sides.note: The text names no school; the commentators identify them with those devoted to the ritual portion of the Veda.

sides.position: Those carried away by that speech do not have resolute understanding established in samādhi; the Vedas deal with the three guṇas, and one should be free of them; for the knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well in a flood.
arguments: Attachment to enjoyment and power prevents resolute understanding in samādhi (2.44).
The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain; be free of the three guṇas and of the pairs of opposites (2.45).
For the knower the Vedas hold no more use than a well amid a flood (2.46).
Understanding must become indifferent to what is heard and stand immovable in samādhi (2.52–53).

notes: The vedavādins' own texts are not part of this chunk; their side is recorded as the Gītā reports it. The commentators divide on how sharply 2.45–46 limit the Veda (see the notes on those teachings).

question: If understanding (buddhi) is superior to action, should one abstain from action?

sides.position: If Kṛṣṇa holds understanding superior to action, it is unclear why he urges terrible action; his words seem mixed, and Arjuna asks for the one thing that leads to the good.
arguments: 2.49 said action is far inferior to buddhiyoga, yet Arjuna is urged to fight (3.1).
The teaching seems mixed and confuses the understanding (3.2).

sides.position: There are two commitments, jñānayoga for the Sāṃkhyas and karmayoga for the Yogins; freedom from action is not reached by not acting, nor perfection by renunciation alone; one must act, for sacrifice and for holding the world together, without attachment.
arguments: No one attains naiṣkarmya by not undertaking actions, nor perfection by mere renunciation (3.4).
No one can remain without acting even a moment; the guṇas make all act (3.5).
Outward restraint while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy (3.6); action is better than inaction and even bodily life needs it (3.8).
Action for sacrifice done unattached does not bind (3.9); acting unattached one attains the highest (3.19).
Janaka and others reached perfection by action; act for lokasaṃgraha, as Kṛṣṇa himself does (3.20–26).

notes: A text-internal debate. It bears on the general debate dsp:works-knowledge-grace, for which the commentaries on these verses are principal sources; the one content in the self is said to have nothing to do (3.17–18).
